lines.text: Write an ordinary-looking function, mark it with the keyword that turns it into one of these lazy computations, and call it, but don't wait on it yet.
In that exact moment, right after the call and before anything else, has any part of its body actually started running?
No, nothing has started — a value comes back, and that's all that happened.
This is the same rule from last time, just reached by a shorter path: the keyword is sugar over building exactly that kind of lazy value, not an exception to how it behaves.

lines.text: So what does that convenient syntax actually turn into, underneath? The language's own specification says it plainly: a plain, anonymous piece of data — and describes its rough shape directly.
One labeled slot for every single pause point in the function, and each one holds exactly whatever local variables are still alive right there.
Take two functions, identical except for one thing: right before the exact same pause point, one of them sets aside a sizeable chunk of local data that has to stay alive across it.
Does keeping that extra data alive across the pause point change how big the resulting value actually is?

lines.text: Yes, it genuinely does.
Whatever's still alive at that pause point has to be stored somewhere inside that one labeled slot, and a bigger local simply means a bigger slot to hold it.
Measure both of these directly, with no need to run either one at all — just ask how many bytes each value actually takes up, right after it's built.
One comes back tiny, just about nothing. The other comes back holding over four thousand times that, because it's dragging that whole chunk of data along with it.
That difference in size isn't just a number sitting in a report somewhere — every single time a value like that one actually moves, every one of those bytes gets copied along with it.
Move it onto the heap, hand it to something that will run it later, and that whole, larger block travels with it, every time.
Now swap that local for something else: a kind of reference-counted handle that was never designed to be handed safely from one thread to another.
Keep that same kind of handle alive across the identical pause point as before — does that cause any trouble at all?
No, it is not fine at all — this genuinely breaks.

Whatever ends up stored inside one of those labeled slots carries its own properties along with it, and a slot holding something unsafe to move between threads makes the whole value unsafe to move between threads too.
Try to actually compile that, and the compiler doesn't just quietly allow it — it refuses outright, and names exactly why.
It points at the handle itself, and at the exact pause point where that handle is still alive, and says plainly that the whole thing can't be handed safely between threads.

A function that looked entirely ordinary turns out to lower, underneath, to a real, inspectable value with real, measurable size — and everything already true about ordinary values turns out to still be true about this one.

That value, built from a chain of these labeled slots, is only simple as long as nothing inside one slot ever points at something else living in a different slot of the exact same value. What happens when it does?
